prompt: Stock rotation uses

options.text: LIFO (last in, first out) so the freshest packs reach the OR
FIFO (first in, first out) so older sterile packs are used first
Rotation by tray weight so heavier sets are used before lighter ones
Rotation by surgeon preference so frequently used sets stay in front

explanation: First in, first out puts the oldest sterile stock ahead of newer stock of the same item, so the older pack is issued first. Last in, first out leaves those older packs at the back, where handling is more likely to damage them. Tray weight and which surgeon likes the set do not decide the order.

distractorExplanations.a: LIFO leaves older packs at the back to outdate or be damaged; sterile stock rotates first in, first out.
distractorExplanations.c: Weight has no bearing on stock rotation; date or lot order (FIFO) determines which packs are used first.
distractorExplanations.d: Preference-based placement ignores dating; FIFO ensures older sterile items are used before newer ones.

The BI result for the load, which must be read before any pack is issued to the OR

distractorExplanations.b: Opening a pack to see the internal CI breaks sterility; the internal CI is read by the scrub person at point of use.

prompt: Wrapped packs are dry but still hot when the sterilizer cart is unloaded. A technician wants the cart cleared before the packs have cooled. What should be done with these packs?

options.text: Bag each hot pack so dust cannot settle, then place the closed bags on the sterile shelf.
Set the hot packs on the sterile shelf against an outside window so moving air cools them.
Stack the hot packs on the sterile shelf now so the unload cart can go back into service.
Leave the packs uncovered until they have cooled, then store them.

distractorExplanations.a: A dust cover or bag on a hot pack traps vapor against the wrap. Cover a pack only after it has cooled and is still dry.
distractorExplanations.b: An outside window brings condensation and is not where hot packs cool. They cool uncovered on the unload cart, then move to dry storage.
distractorExplanations.c: Putting hot packs on the shelf to free a cart stores them before they are cool and dry. Cooling belongs on the unload cart, not on the sterile shelf.

prompt: Event-related sterility means sterility is maintained until

options.text: The fixed expiration date printed on the label is reached
An event compromises the package (eg, moisture, tears, improper handling)
The sterilizer that processed the load is next taken out of service for repair
The outside of an intact wrap is touched during ordinary handling

explanation: Event-related sterility holds while the barrier stays intact. It ends when an event compromises the package, such as moisture, a tear, or handling that damages the pack. A printed expiration date, taking the sterilizer out of service, and a routine touch of an intact wrap do not end it.

distractorExplanations.a: Fixed calendar dating is time-related sterility; event-related sterility depends on package condition, not a date.
distractorExplanations.c: Equipment service does not outdate stored packages; a compromising event or facility policy does.
distractorExplanations.d: Touching the outside of an intact wrap during ordinary handling does not break the barrier. Event-related sterility ends on a real compromise, such as moisture, a tear, or a hole.

Use the same cart that returns soiled instruments, wiped down between the trips

A cart that carried soiled instruments is cleaned before it is used for sterile packs. Wiping the shelves between those trips does not change a soiled cart into a clean one.

distractorExplanations.a: Open carts expose packs to dust and contact; sterile items move in covered or enclosed carts.
distractorExplanations.c: Heavy trays crush peel packs and stacking compresses wrap; packages are placed to avoid compression and punctures.

Ensure that newer stock is used first because it was sterilized more recently

Remove the need to check expiration dates when items are issued

distractorExplanations.b: That describes LIFO; FIFO rotates older stock forward so it is used before it expires or is damaged.

prompt: If a sterile package falls on the floor, best practice is generally to:

options.text: Wipe the outside with a hospital disinfectant and return the pack to sterile storage for the next case
Consider it contaminated and reprocess according to facility policy
Use it if the outer wrap is dry and has no visible tears
Relabel it with a new load sticker and return it to the shelf

explanation: A sterile package that hits the floor is treated as contaminated and goes back for reprocessing. The impact can force soil through a wrap that still looks dry and untorn, so appearance does not clear it. A disinfectant wipe and a new load label do not reprocess the pack. Facility policy is the path for that reprocessing, not a reason to put the pack back on the shelf.

distractorExplanations.a: Disinfectant wiping cannot reverse contamination from floor contact; the pack must be reprocessed.
distractorExplanations.c: A dropped pack can have unseen damage, and impact can force contaminants through wrap; appearance does not clear it.
distractorExplanations.d: A new label does not reprocess the item; the contaminated pack must be unwrapped, inspected and resterilized.

prompt: A technician rotating the suture shelf finds a sealed pack that is dry, with no hole and no broken seal. A coworker wants it discarded because the sterilization date looks old. What should happen to that pack?

options.text: Keep the intact pack in sterile storage, and use the sterilization date to rotate stock.
Discard the pack, because an old sterilization date ends shelf life even when the wrap and seal are intact.
Wipe the wrap with disinfectant and move the pack in front of the newer suture stock.
Open a corner to read the internal indicator, then tape the pack shut if the indicator changed.

explanation: Event-related sterility means the pack stays sterile until an event compromises it, such as a hole, moisture, or a broken seal. An older sterilization date, with the barrier still intact, is not that event. The date remains so staff can rotate first in, first out and trace the pack to its load.

distractorExplanations.b: An older sterilization date supports rotation and traceability. It does not, by itself, end sterility when the seal, wrap, and dryness are intact.
distractorExplanations.c: Wiping a wrap with disinfectant does not decide sterility, and moving an older pack to the front reverses first-in, first-out rotation.
distractorExplanations.d: Opening the pack breaks the barrier. Tape cannot make that pack sterile again, and the internal indicator is read at use, not in storage.

prompt: Two sterile wrapped hernia sets sit on the same shelf, and the afternoon hernia repair needs one of them. Both sets are dry and sealed. The set at the back was sterilized before the set in front. Which set should go to the repair?

options.text: Issue the front set, because the more recently sterilized pack is the safer one to send into the operating room.
Issue the lighter set, because rotation follows tray weight rather than which set was sterilized first.
Issue the set that was sterilized earlier, not the one in front, so the older intact stock is used first.
Issue either set, because event-related sterility makes sterilization order irrelevant to the pick.

explanation: First in, first out issues the older sterile set before the newer one when both are dry and sealed. The set sterilized earlier is the one that goes to the hernia repair. Taking the front set because it is newer leaves the older intact set on the shelf.

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing the more recently sterilized set is last-in, first-out. It leaves the older intact set behind and defeats stock rotation.
distractorExplanations.b: Tray weight has nothing to do with which sterile set is issued. Rotation follows which set was sterilized first when both have passed inspection.
distractorExplanations.d: Event-related sterility decides whether a pack is still sterile, not which intact pack is issued first. First in, first out still selects the earlier set.

prompt: While pulling a minor tray for the next case, the technician sees a small hole in the outer wrap of the tray just taken off the shelf. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Cover the hole with sterilization tape, initial the repair, and load the tray so the case is not delayed.
Take off the outer wrap and issue the inner wrap if that layer has no hole of its own.
Do not load the tray now. Slide it to the back of the same shelf and leave it in sterile storage.
Do not issue the tray or leave it on the shelf. Send it back to decontamination for reprocessing.

explanation: A hole in the wrap is an event that ends sterility for that package. Both layers of a wrapped tray are part of the barrier, so a hole in the outer wrap is enough. Tape cannot close it, and unwrapping the tray in storage is not a way to issue it. The tray goes back to decontamination to be reprocessed.

distractorExplanations.a: Sterilization tape does not patch a hole in a wrap. A torn pack is compromised and is not loaded onto a case cart to save time.
distractorExplanations.b: Both wrap layers form the barrier. A hole in the outer layer compromises the pack, and the inner layer is not issued from the storeroom.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving the tray to the back of the shelf leaves a compromised pack in sterile storage, where someone else can pick it later.

prompt: The afternoon runner reaches the service elevator with a closed cart of sterile packs and a second cart of uncovered soiled instruments from the same floor. How should the runner move the two loads?

options.text: Stack the sterile packs on the soiled cart and take both loads up on one trip.
Set the sterile packs on the elevator floor and use the closed cart for the soiled instruments.
Route the closed sterile cart through decontamination so it can follow the soiled cart on one path.
Take the closed sterile cart on its own trip, separate from the uncovered soiled cart.

explanation: Clean and soiled transport stay separate. Uncovered soiled instruments are not taken on the same trip as a sterile delivery, and sterile packs are not stacked onto the soiled cart or set on the elevator floor. The closed sterile cart goes by itself. The soiled cart returns by the soiled path, not by pulling the sterile cart through decontamination.

distractorExplanations.a: Sterile packs do not ride on a cart of uncovered soiled instruments. Combining the loads contaminates the delivery.
distractorExplanations.b: The elevator floor is a dirty surface. Sterile packs are not set there so a cart can be reused for soiled instruments.
distractorExplanations.c: A sterile delivery does not detour through decontamination to share a route with soiled instruments. The loads stay apart.

prompt: A knee case cart is nearly closed. The technician sees a shoulder arthroscopy set on it, while the pick list names the knee arthroscopy set. What should the technician do before closing the cart?

options.text: Remove the shoulder set, return it to stock, and load the knee set named on the pick list.
Send the cart as it is and have the operating room call back if the shoulder set is not what the knee case needs.
Send the shoulder set to decontamination and release the cart with whatever sets remain on it.
Relabel the shoulder set with the knee set name so the ticket matches the tray that was picked.

explanation: A case cart is accurate when the sets on it match the pick list for that case. A shoulder arthroscopy set does not fill a line that names the knee set. The wrong set comes off and returns to stock, the named set is inspected and loaded, and the cart is closed only after that match.

distractorExplanations.b: The operating room should receive the set the pick list named. Sending the wrong tray and waiting for a callback is a case-cart error.
distractorExplanations.c: The shoulder set is not compromised, so decontamination is the wrong destination, and releasing a cart that is missing the knee set is still inaccurate.
distractorExplanations.d: Relabeling the wrong set makes the ticket lie. The cart has to hold the set the case actually requested.

prompt: A wrapped basin set shows a faint moisture stain on the outside wrap while the set is still sitting in sterile storage. What is the correct handling of this set?

options.text: Issue the set if the stain is faint and the load label can still be read without trouble.
Do not involve decontamination. Blot the stain with a dry towel and put the set back on the shelf.
Do not issue the stained set. Remove it from storage and send it to decontamination.
Release the set, because an outside stain does not matter after the basins have already been sterilized.

explanation: Moisture on a sterile wrap is a compromising event, including a faint stain, because liquid can carry contamination through the barrier. The set is not blotted and returned to the shelf, and it is not issued because the basins were sterilized earlier. It comes out of storage and goes to decontamination.

distractorExplanations.a: A faint stain, or a label that can still be read, does not clear moisture on the wrap. Moisture is a compromising event.
distractorExplanations.b: Blotting the wrap and putting the set back on the shelf leaves a compromised pack in sterile storage. Drying the outside does not undo the stain.
distractorExplanations.d: An earlier sterilization cycle does not protect a pack after the barrier is wet. A moisture stain means the set is not issued.

prompt: One corner of a peel pouch holding a light cord has a lifted seal. The pouch is still in its bin, and the rest of the pouch looks flat. What should staff do with this pouch?

options.text: Press the lifted corner shut with a finger and issue the pouch if the plastic stays down.
Run the open corner through the heat sealer in sterile storage and return the pouch to its bin.
Do not reseal or issue the pouch. Remove it from the bin and send it to decontamination.
Put the pouch on the next case cart and tell the scrub person to watch that corner during opening.

explanation: A peel-pouch seal is part of the sterile barrier. A lifted corner means that barrier is open, even if the rest of the pouch looks flat. Pressing it shut or sealing it again in storage does not reprocess the cord. The pouch is removed and sent to decontamination rather than placed on a cart.

distractorExplanations.a: Finger pressure does not restore a peel-pouch seal. A lifted corner means the barrier is already open.
distractorExplanations.b: Sealing the corner again, without cleaning the contents, does not reprocess the pouch. The open seal already compromised the item.
distractorExplanations.d: Asking the scrub person to watch the corner still issues a pouch with a broken seal. That pouch does not leave the shelf.

prompt: Freshly sterilized packs of the same gauze lot are cooled and ready for a shelf that already holds older intact packs of that lot. How should the new packs be placed?

options.text: Place the new packs in front so the operating room receives the gauze that was sterilized most recently.
Mix the new packs through the older packs so the shelf no longer shows which date should go first.
Leave the new packs on the sterilizer rack until every older pack in the bin has been issued.
Place the new packs behind the older intact packs so the older gauze is issued first.

explanation: First in, first out is done on the shelf: newer packs of the same item go behind older intact packs, so the older packs are picked first. Putting the new packs in front, or mixing the dates, hides the older stock. Cooled packs are not left on the sterilizer rack instead of being rotated.

distractorExplanations.a: Putting the new packs in front issues the newest stock first. That is last-in, first-out, and the older packs stay buried.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixing dates at random means the picker cannot tell which pack was sterilized first, so first-in, first-out fails.
distractorExplanations.c: Cooled sterile packs belong in storage, behind the older packs of that item. Leaving them on the sterilizer rack is not stock rotation.

prompt: A cart that carried soiled instruments this morning was wiped with a dry cloth. It is the only free cart for a sterile delivery to labor and delivery. What is the correct use of this cart?

options.text: Load the sterile packs onto it, because a dry wipe is enough to switch the cart from a soiled trip to a clean one.
Line the shelves with a clean sheet and then load the sterile packs onto that same cart for the trip.
Put the sterile packs in open baskets on that cart so staff can see that the load itself is clean.
Do not load this cart. Send it to be cleaned, and take the sterile packs on a clean closed cart.

explanation: A cart that carried soiled instruments stays a soiled cart until it has been cleaned for a clean role. A dry wipe, a sheet, or an open basket does not make that change. Sterile packs go out on a clean closed cart, and this cart is sent for cleaning instead of being loaded.

distractorExplanations.a: A dry cloth wipe does not clean a cart that carried soiled instruments. That cart is not ready for a sterile delivery.
distractorExplanations.b: A clean sheet on a soiled cart does not change the cart's role. Soiled transport and sterile transport stay separate.
distractorExplanations.c: Open baskets expose the packs, and the packs would still be riding on a cart that was used for soiled instruments.

prompt: An assembled case cart sits at the storeroom door. The technician has not compared the sets on the cart with the pick ticket. What has to happen before the cart is released?

options.text: Match each loaded set to the pick ticket and correct any miss before the cart leaves.
Send the cart now and let the circulating nurse reconcile the sets after the patient is in the room.
Count the trays, and release the cart if that count equals the number of lines printed on the ticket.
Sign the ticket complete, because an experienced technician assembled the cart earlier in the shift.

explanation: Case-cart accuracy means the sets on the cart are the sets on the pick ticket, checked before the cart leaves the storeroom. A tray count can match while the identities are wrong. The check is not skipped because of who built the cart, and it is not left for the circulating nurse to discover in the room.

distractorExplanations.b: Case-cart accuracy is checked before the cart leaves sterile storage. The circulating nurse should not be the first person to find a wrong set.
distractorExplanations.c: A matching tray count can still hide the wrong set. Each line on the pick ticket has to match the set that was actually loaded.
distractorExplanations.d: Who built the cart does not prove the contents. The ticket is compared with the sets on the cart before the cart is released.

prompt: A new employee is about to hand a sterile pack to the runner after checking only that a load label is on the wrap. What should the employee do before handing the pack over?

options.text: Hand it over. The load label shows the pack was already inspected when the sterilizer was unloaded.
Open a corner, read the internal indicator, tape the pack shut, and then hand it to the runner.
Check the pack for holes, moisture, and a broken seal before it leaves the shelf.
Hand it over now, because the operating room has already called and is waiting on this pack.

explanation: Before a pack leaves the shelf, the person issuing it looks for holes, moisture, and a broken seal. The load label ties the pack to its cycle, but it cannot show damage that happened in storage. The pack is not opened to read the internal indicator, and a rush call does not cancel the look.

distractorExplanations.a: The load label identifies the cycle. It does not show a hole, a wet spot, or a seal that failed after the pack was stored.
distractorExplanations.b: Opening the pack in the storeroom breaks the barrier. The internal indicator is read at the point of use, not by unsealing the pack for the runner.
distractorExplanations.d: A call from the room does not skip the inspection. A pack with a hole, moisture, or a broken seal is not issued to save time.

prompt: A coworker offers sterilization tape to close a torn corner on a wrapped pack the operating room says it needs within minutes. What is the correct response?

options.text: Tape the tear and issue the pack, because sterilization tape restores the barrier in time for the waiting case.
Tape the tear, apply a new load label over the repair, and place the pack on the cart that is about to leave.
Issue the pack with the tear left open, since the case cannot wait and the damage sits at the corner.
Refuse the tape and do not issue the torn pack. Send it back to decontamination for reprocessing.

explanation: A torn wrap is a compromised pack. Sterilization tape does not rebuild that barrier, and a new label does not reprocess the set. Time pressure from the operating room does not justify issuing the tear, whether it is taped or left open. The pack goes back to decontamination.

distractorExplanations.a: Sterilization tape is an external process indicator and a closure aid when a pack is wrapped. It does not repair a tear in a pack that is already on the shelf.
distractorExplanations.b: A new load label over tape does not reprocess a torn pack. The barrier is already broken, so the pack is not placed on the cart.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaving the tear open and issuing the pack still sends a compromised barrier to the case. Urgency does not change the disposition.

prompt: A rigid container on the sterile shelf has an open latch and a broken tamper-evident seal. The container was not dropped. What should be done with this container?

options.text: Close the latch, apply a new seal, and leave the container in sterile storage for the next pick.
Wipe the outside and issue the container if the filter housing on the lid looks undamaged.
Issue the container for the waiting case, then send it for processing after that procedure ends.
Do not issue the container. The broken seal sends the set back to decontamination.

explanation: The latch and the tamper-evident seal show that a rigid container stayed closed after sterilization. An open latch and a broken seal are a compromising event, whether or not the container was dropped. Relatching it in storage, wiping the outside, or sending it for this case does not restore sterility. The set goes back to decontamination.

distractorExplanations.a: Closing the latch and hanging a new seal in storage does not sterilize the set. The broken seal means the container was open after processing.
distractorExplanations.b: Wiping the outside does not address an open latch and a broken tamper seal. The set is not issued in that condition.
distractorExplanations.c: Using the container for the case and processing it afterward still sends a compromised set into the procedure.

prompt: The cardiac case cart was labeled for operating room 4. The runner is told to leave it in room 6 because that room is closer to the elevator. Where should this cart go?

options.text: Leave it in room 6 and change the cart label so the paperwork matches the closer room.
Park it in the corridor between room 4 and room 6 so either circulating nurse can take it.
Deliver the cart to operating room 4, the room named on the case-cart label.
Take the cart back and rebuild those sets under a new pick ticket written for room 6.

explanation: Case-cart distribution is accurate when the cart reaches the case it was built for. This cart is labeled for room 4, so that is where it goes. Moving the label to room 6, leaving the cart in the corridor, or rebuilding it for the closer room assigns the sets to the wrong case.

distractorExplanations.a: Changing the label to room 6 sends the cardiac cart to the wrong case. A shorter walk does not reassign a cart that was already built.
distractorExplanations.b: A cart parked in the corridor is not a delivery, and either room taking it can open another case's sets.
distractorExplanations.d: Rebuilding the cart under a room 6 ticket assigns those sets to the wrong case. The label already names room 4.

prompt: An unused pack comes back from the operating room with the outer wrap opened and then folded closed. The instruments inside were not used. What is the correct disposition of the pack?

options.text: Refold the wrap, close it with sterilization tape, and return the pack to the shelf location it came from.
Put the pack back into sterile storage, because the instruments never touched the sterile field during the case.
Place the unused pack on the next case cart without reprocessing, so the same preparation is not repeated.
Send the pack to decontamination. Folding the opened wrap shut does not restore the barrier.

explanation: Once the outer wrap is opened, the sterile barrier is broken, even if the instruments were not used and someone folds the wrap closed again. Tape does not make that pack stock again. An unopened pack whose barrier is still intact can be inspected and returned; this wrap was opened, so reprocessing starts in decontamination.

distractorExplanations.a: Tape and a refold do not recreate a sterile barrier after the wrap has been opened. The pack is not returned to the shelf.
distractorExplanations.b: Instruments that never touched the field are still treated as contaminated once the wrap is opened. Non-use does not keep the pack sterile.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving the opened pack onto another cart skips reprocessing. An opened wrap is a compromised pack and does not stay in distribution.
